text:
The train from the city took four hours, and my mother, who had not driven in three years, was waiting at the station in the passenger seat of her neighbor's Buick, waving before the train had fully stopped, as though I might otherwise fail to recognize her. She was eighty-one. She wore the straw hat with the faded blue ribbon and a blouse I remembered from a photograph taken in the nineties—my mother had entered a phase of life in which clothing did not wear out so much as deepen, like timber.

"You look thin," she said, which was her way of saying hello. I had gained eleven pounds since Christmas.

Doris, the neighbor, drove us the six blocks to the house, refusing my offer of gas money with the practiced offense of a woman who considered generosity a competitive sport. Their arrangement: Doris drove, and my mother pretended to navigate, calling out turns Doris had already made.

The house was the house. The same maple my father had threatened to cut down every autumn for twenty years and never did; the same porch swing with the chain that bit your palm if you gripped it wrong; the same smell inside, which I can only describe as the smell of a place where one person has lived long enough to become part of the ventilation—cinnamon, furniture polish, and something older and sweeter underneath, like the ghost of every meal ever cooked there, paying rent.

She had made a ham. I had told her on the phone, twice, that we could go out for lunch, and she had agreed in the way she agreed to most things, which was to say not at all. The ham sat under a tent of foil, scalloped potatoes keeping it company in the oven, and a Jell-O salad with shredded carrots suspended in it like artifacts in amber—a dish I had not encountered since the Reagan administration and had not missed but was strangely moved to see.

"Just a little something," she said.

We ate at the kitchen table, the good dining room table being reserved, as always, for an occasion that had not yet occurred in forty years. Over lunch she gave me the news of the town, structured like a liturgy: who had died, who was dying, who had sold to people from the city. The Kessler boy—who was fifty-four—had bought a boat. Nobody knew what he intended to do with it.

After lunch she showed me the garden, which was not really a garden anymore but a treaty between my mother and entropy, renegotiated each spring with diminishing territory. She bent over the tomato cages with the slow ceremony of a woman laying wreaths, and told me, as she told me every visit, why the Early Girls were a concession to the shortening patience of old age.

"Your father always said plant late and plant deep," she said. "Your father also said he was going to fix the gutter." She pointed at the gutter, which hung from the garage at the angle of a shrug. My father had been dead eleven years. I offered to fix it. She said not to be foolish, I didn't know anything about gutters. This was true, but it was not, I felt, the point.

We sat on the porch in the afternoon, minding the chain. It was June, and hot—the kind of heat that makes a small town go quiet in the middle of the day. We drank iced tea from mason jars. We talked the way porch conversations move in families, returning always to the same channels: my work, my apartment, whether I was seeing anyone, and then, at last, the old country—her childhood, the farm, her mother, who I knew mostly as a stern presence in sepia and a recipe for rolls no one had ever successfully reproduced.

"She could carry two full buckets from the well and not spill a drop," my mother said. "I used to try it. I'd get to the porch with half a bucket and my dress soaked. She never once said a word about it. Just handed me the rag."

I had heard this story before. There was a time in my thirties when this repetition had felt like erosion, evidence that our relationship had worn down to a few smooth stones we passed back and forth. I understand it differently now. The stories are the stones, yes, but the passing back and forth is the point. She was not informing me of anything. She was handing me something and watching to see that I took it.

In the evening we watched a nature program about the deep ocean, which my mother narrated over with commentary of her own. She distrusted octopuses. She felt the anglerfish had been treated unfairly by God. At nine she announced she was exhausted, in the manner of an empress dismissing the court, and went to bed.

I walked through the house before I slept, reading it. The photographs on the hallway wall: my parents' wedding, me at various ages, my hair a series of historical misjudgments. My father's Louis L'Amour paperbacks, which my mother would not discard and would never read. In the bathroom, her pills in a plastic organizer with the days of the week in raised letters, an object I still could not look at directly.

In the morning she made pancakes, because when I was eight I had loved pancakes. I ate four. She watched me eat them with an expression of undiluted triumph, as though she had solved me. Perhaps she had. Then Doris arrived with the Buick, and my mother stood on the porch and told me to eat more, call more, visit more, and be careful on the train, as though the train were a thing I would be operating personally. I hugged her, and she was smaller than the hug I had prepared, and I watched her in the side mirror until the turn took her away, still standing there, one hand on the porch post.

I remember thinking, on the train, that I should come back sooner. A month is not a long time. It is the length of a billing cycle. It is the time between haircuts.

The call came on a Tuesday, from Doris, whose voice had changed into something efficient. Sunstroke. My mother had been in the garden at two in the afternoon in a heat advisory, watering the tomatoes, because—and Doris delivered this with furious tenderness—she said the plants were confused by the heat and needed her. She was at the county hospital. She was stable. She was, Doris said, extremely angry about the tomatoes.

I got there the next morning. She was small in the hospital bed in a way she had never been small in her own house, the machinery of care arranged around her like scaffolding around a building everyone had assumed was permanent. She was lucid, then tired, then lucid again. She told me the IV itched. She told me the doctor was twelve. She told me, in a moment of awful clarity, "I got too hot," as though reporting a minor mechanical failure, and then she slept, and the room did that thing hospital rooms do, which is to remove all sense of time's direction.

She would recover, the twelve-year-old doctor said. "She's strong," he said, as though I might dispute it. I wanted to tell him about the buckets from the well.

In the afternoon I drove to the house to get her things. My key from college still worked, and the door opened onto the smell, cinnamon and polish and ghost, and I stood in the hallway a moment because the house did not know.

The evidence was everywhere, once I looked. On the counter, her grocery list in her upright schoolteacher's hand, and at the bottom, "fruit for R.," my initial, the list from the weekend of my visit, saved now for reasons that were not practical. In the refrigerator, the last of the Jell-O salad, which she had not been able to throw away and could no longer eat. The mason jars, washed and turned upside down on a dish towel—both of them, hers and mine, drained together. On the coffee table, her crossword book open to a half-finished puzzle, and beside it, squared with the corner of the table the way she squared everything, the letter I had sent her at Easter and a photograph she must have taken down from the hallway: me at nine, squinting into the sun, holding a fish I had not caught but had been allowed to pose with. She had been looking at these. In the evenings, with the cat, she had been looking at these.

I sat down on the sofa. The cat materialized, inspected me, and, finding no better offer, climbed into my lap.

Out the window I could see the garden. The tomatoes had not died. Doris or someone had watered them—the neighbors ran a quiet government of their own in that town—and the plants stood in their cages, heavy and green, ripening without her. The gutter hung off the garage. The porch swing moved a little in no wind. Everything she had touched was holding its shape, the way a held note holds after the singer has stopped, and I understood that this was what I had actually been given, all those visits, all those pancakes and mason jars of tea: not nostalgia, which is what I had condescendingly assumed, but a record. She had been keeping the place like a lantern. The old habits were not habits. They were maintenance. She was maintaining a world so that there would be something solid to come back to, something with my initial on the grocery list.

I packed her bag. I fed the cat. I took the photograph of the boy with the fish off the coffee table and put it in the bag, because I thought she might want it, or because I thought she might have wanted me to want it, which amounts, in our family, to the same thing.

At the hospital she was awake, quarreling mildly with a nurse about the Jell-O on her dinner tray, which was the wrong color and contained, she reported, no carrots of any kind. She saw the photograph sticking up out of the bag.

"You went in the house," she said, with the air of a woman catching a known thief.

"Doris has been feeding the cat," I said. "The tomatoes are fine."

"The tomatoes are not fine. Nobody waters them right but me." She took the photograph from me and squared it against the blanket with both hands. "You caught that fish," she said.

"You know I didn't."

"You held it like you caught it," she said. "That's something."

She slept again after a while, and I stayed in the chair. Outside the window the evening came down over the parking lot, the ordinary dusk of an ordinary day that had nearly gone another way, and I thought about the house holding its shape, and the note in the air, and how long a person can carry two buckets and spill how much and still arrive. I would fix the gutter, I decided. I didn't know anything about gutters. I would learn.
